subject: mathematics_1b
question_text: Show that the tangent at any point θ on the curve x = c sec θ, y = c tan θ is y sin θ = x − c cos θ.

mark_split.label: Differentiate x and y with respect to θ
Write the tangent at the point

recall_prompt: Say how you would show this — say how you get dy/dx for a curve given through θ, what that slope simplifies to, and which identity you use at the end.

steps.label: Differentiate x and y with respect to θ
steps.margin_note: First mark. Both derivatives are with respect to θ, not x. c is a constant and stays in front of both.
lines: Given:   x = c sec θ,   y = c tan θ
Differentiate each with respect to θ:
dx/dθ = c sec θ tan θ

recall.must_convey: That dx/dθ = c sec θ tan θ and dy/dθ = c sec²θ.
accept: differentiate both x and y with respect to theta
sec theta differentiates to sec theta tan theta
tan theta differentiates to sec squared theta
theta tho rendu ni differentiate cheyyali
dx by d theta is c sec theta tan theta
dy by d theta is c sec squared theta

steps.why: The curve is given through a parameter, so x and y cannot be differentiated against each other directly. Each is differentiated against θ first, and the two results are combined in the next step.
common_mistakes: Differentiating sec θ to sec θ only, leaving out the tan θ factor.
Differentiating tan θ to sec θ instead of sec²θ.
Differentiating with respect to x, which the parametric form does not allow.
steps.memory_tip: sec differentiates to sec times tan; tan differentiates to sec squared. Both keep sec in the answer.

steps.label: Slope of the tangent
steps.margin_note: Second mark. c cancels, and one sec θ cancels with the sec²θ above it. Writing sec θ and tan θ in terms of sin and cos makes the final form obvious.
lines: For a curve given through θ:   dy/dx = (dy/dθ) / (dx/dθ)
dy/dx = c sec²θ / (c sec θ tan θ)

accept: dy by dx is dy by d theta divided by dx by d theta
c cancels and one sec theta cancels
the slope is one by sin theta
dy by d theta ni dx by d theta tho divide cheyyali
sec theta by tan theta is cosec theta
the slope is cosec theta

steps.why: Dividing the two θ-derivatives cancels dθ and gives the slope in terms of θ alone. Converting to sin and cos at this point is what makes the last step short.
common_mistakes: Writing dy/dx as (dx/dθ)/(dy/dθ), the two the wrong way round.
Simplifying sec θ/tan θ to cos θ instead of cosec θ.
Leaving c in the slope after it has cancelled.
steps.memory_tip: Divide the y-derivative by the x-derivative — the letter on top matches the letter on top of dy/dx.

steps.label: Write the tangent at the point
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The point is the parametric pair itself, (c sec θ, c tan θ). Multiplying through by sin θ removes the fraction and moves the working towards the printed form.
lines: The point on the curve at parameter θ is  (c sec θ, c tan θ).
Tangent at (x₁, y₁) with slope m:   y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
y − c tan θ = (1/sin θ)(x − c sec θ)
Multiply both sides by sin θ:
y sin θ − c tan θ sin θ = x − c sec θ

recall.must_convey: That the point is (c sec θ, c tan θ) and multiplying the point-slope form by sin θ gives y sin θ − c tan θ sin θ = x − c sec θ.
accept: the point is c sec theta comma c tan theta
use the point slope form with slope one by sin theta
multiply both sides by sin theta
sin theta tho rendu vaipula multiply cheyyali
y sin theta minus c tan theta sin theta equals x minus c sec theta
write the tangent at the parametric point

steps.why: The required form has y sin θ on the left, so multiplying by sin θ at this stage puts the working on the same shape as the target and leaves only the constant terms to simplify.
common_mistakes: Using (c tan θ, c sec θ), swapping the coordinates.
Multiplying only the left side by sin θ.
Expanding (1/sin θ)(x − c sec θ) term by term and losing the c sec θ.
steps.memory_tip: Look at the printed answer first. It has y sin θ on the left, so multiply by sin θ as soon as the line is written.

steps.label: Simplify to the required form
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. This is where sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 is used. Take c cos θ out of the two constant terms and the bracket that is left equals 1.
lines: y sin θ = x − c sec θ + c tan θ sin θ
= x − (c sec θ − c tan θ sin θ)
Now  sec θ = sec²θ · cos θ  and  tan θ sin θ = tan²θ · cos θ,  so
c sec θ − c tan θ sin θ = c cos θ (sec²θ − tan²θ)
Since sec²θ − tan²θ = 1, this equals c cos θ.

lines.text: ∴ y sin θ = x − c cos θ

recall.must_convey: That c sec θ − c tan θ sin θ = c cos θ(sec²θ − tan²θ) = c cos θ, giving y sin θ = x − c cos θ.
accept: take c cos theta common from the two terms
sec squared theta minus tan squared theta is one
the two constant terms come to c cos theta
sec square minus tan square equal to one use cheyyali
that leaves y sin theta equals x minus c cos theta
the identity finishes the proof

steps.why: Both constant terms carry a cos θ once sec θ and tan θ sin θ are rewritten, so c cos θ comes out as a common factor and the standard identity reduces the bracket to 1. The same result follows from 1 − sin²θ = cos²θ.
common_mistakes: Using sec²θ + tan²θ = 1, which is not an identity.
Losing the minus sign when moving −c tan θ sin θ across the equals sign.
Stopping at x − c(1 − sin²θ)/cos θ without reducing it to c cos θ.
steps.memory_tip: sec²θ − tan²θ = 1 comes straight from 1 + tan²θ = sec²θ. Whenever sec and tan appear squared together, that identity is the one to use.

insider_note: Parametric, so dy/dx = (dy/dθ)/(dx/dθ), and it simplifies to cosec θ. Multiplying through by sin θ at the end is what produces the printed form.
